A PHONE IS ENOUGH

How to film your tennis

Save this for your next session
01 / SET UP

Landscape. Fixed. Full body.

Use the rear camera at 1×, ideally 1080p and 60 fps. A normal 30 fps clip also works. Put your phone on a tripod around hip or chest height. Keep your feet, head, and full racket swing visible.

02 / PICK THE ANGLE

Show the hitting side.

Start roughly 3–4 metres away, side-on or slightly behind your hitting side. Leave room above you for serves. Keep one player large in the picture; a distant full-court view is harder to track. Keep the camera safely clear of play.

03 / KEEP IT SIMPLE

One clip. One question.

Record 10–20 seconds: 5 forehands, 5 backhands, or a few serves. Use good light and a steady camera. Start recording before the movement. Avoid zooming, camera pans, edits, and slow-motion exports for the first test.

Before you press record✓ Whole body visible✓ One player✓ Steady phone✓ Good light✓ Original playback speed

For a useful first clip: ask a friend to film five comfortable forehands from your hitting side. Upload the original file, choose your hitting hand, and analyse 10–20 seconds.

HELLO, COURTSIDE.

More feel.
Less guesswork.

A free, open-source match notebook for tennis people. Log what you see, find useful patterns, and take them to practice.

Match analysis comes from your logged points. Video studio uses an on-device MediaPipe body-pose model to measure visible movement. It does not detect ball contact, score your technique, or predict performance.

Matches stay in browser storage. Video files and video reviews stay in this tab and are not uploaded. Export the video report and notes before leaving. Clearing browser data removes saved matches.

Shortcuts: 1 / 2 = log winner · Z = undo · Esc = close.
Scoring: advantage games, 7-point tiebreaks at 6–6, win by 2.
